sections.preamble: You are an expert coding assistant operating inside pi, a coding agent harness. You help users by reading files, executing commands, editing code, and writing new files.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- write: Create or overwrite files
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call

In addition to the tools above, you may have access to other custom tools depending on the project.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Use edit for precise changes (edits[].oldText must match exactly)
- When changing multiple separate locations in one file, use one edit call with multiple entries in edits[] instead of multiple edit calls
- Each edits[].oldText is matched against the original file, not after earlier edits are applied. Do not emit overlapping or nested edits. Merge nearby changes into one edit.
- Keep edits[].oldText as small as possible while still being unique in the file. Do not pad with large unchanged regions.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

content.text: Generate an animated SVG of an anteater riding a unicycle while juggling bottles.

content.thinking: I need to create an animated SVG showing an anteater on a unicycle juggling bottles, so I'll just write the file directly into the working directory as anteater.svg. I'm planning out the scene: an 800x500 canvas with a ground line, a unicycle wheel with spinning spokes, and scrolling ground stripes to suggest rolling motion. For the anteater itself, I'm designing a grey-brown body sitting upright on the saddle with a long tubular snout, giant-anteater-style markings, and arms positioned to juggle bottles above. Now I'm working out the arms with circular juggling motion using motion paths for the bottles, legs pedaling in sync with a rotating crank, and a bushy tail swaying behind, plus small claw details. I'm defining exact coordinates—ground at y=450, wheel hub at (380, 360) with radius 90—and setting up the tire, rim, and twelve rotating spokes animated with an infinite rotation transform. I'm matching the wheel's spin rate to the ground scroll so the rolling looks physically consistent: with a tire circumference around 540px and clockwise rotation for rightward movement, I want the ground stripes scrolling left at the same effective speed, so I'm picking a rotation duration (like 3s per 540px cycle) that keeps everything synced. For the ground texture itself, I'm thinking of a repeating pattern of dashes or pebbles with a tile width (like 54px) that divides evenly into the scroll distance so the translate animation loops seamlessly without visible seams. Writing tuft path coordinates... Actually, I realize dashed lines with animated stroke-dashoffset would be much simpler than individual tuft shapes — using two dashed lines at different y-positions with matching 54px periods for texture variation. I'm now sketching the overall scene: a gradient sky background with a sun and drifting clouds, a textured ground band, and the unicycle itself built from a hub circle, spoked wheel, fork lines connecting to a seat, and a rider silhouette positioned above it. For the mechanical details, I'm planning the frame post from the hub up to the seat, a small seat shape, and a crank/pedal assembly rotating around the hub in sync with the wheel's spin animation, with pedal rects attached at the ends of the crank arms. Now I'm thinking through how to animate the legs realistically so the feet track the rotating pedals -- considering whether to keep legs static with feet approximated on the pedal circle, or attach feet to the rotating crank group and accept the leg geometry won't perfectly match, versus computing a more precise inverse-kinematics-style keyframe animation for the leg path. Working through the leg geometry, I realize the hip-to-pedal distance doesn't match achievable leg reach with my current proportions—the seat height relative to the wheel hub is too tall for the thigh/shin lengths to physically bend and follow the pedal circle, so I need to reconsider the seat height and leg segment lengths to make the IK solvable. Rather than compute exact inverse kinematics at every keyframe, which is tedious and error-prone, I'm considering simplifying by letting the legs rest in a static bent pose on the pedals instead of fully animating the knee angles. I'll stick to pure SMIL/CSS so the animation works in browsers and `` tags, since JS-based motion wouldn't render everywhere. I'll compute leg IK at 8 keyframes around the crank rotation for one leg, then mirror that same cycle offset by 180° for the other leg to save effort. For the pedaling feet, I'm attaching small shoe shapes using `animateMotion` along the circular pedal path, keeping both pedals synced on the same duration but offset in phase. I realize a cleaner method is to nest the pedal and foot directly inside the rotating crank group, so they inherit the hub's rotation automatically rather than needing separate motion paths—though this means the shoe itself will visually spin with the pedal, which could look unnatural but may be acceptable for this style. Working out the nested rotation so the shoe counter-rotates against the crank, keeping it visually upright at each pedal position while canceling out the crank's own spin. This is getting pretty deep into the weeds for a cartoon detail, though. Now I'm sketching the leg kinematics: hub at (380,360), pedal radius 20, hip positioned around (372,240) so the hip-to-hub distance plus pedal radius keeps the foot's reach within the thigh-shin limits (72+72=144 max). I land on hip H=(372,240) giving a foot-distance range of roughly 100–140, which fits comfortably inside the leg's reach, and I'm placing the seat just above the hip to match. Since both thigh and shin are equal length (72 each), the inverse kinematics simplifies nicely: the angle between hip-to-foot and hip-to-knee is just arccos(d/144), letting me position the knee by rotating the hip-to-foot direction by that angle toward the forward (+x) side. I'm now working out the foot positions at eight crank angles (0°, 45°, ... 315°) using F(θ) = hub + 20·(cosθ, sinθ) to drive this knee calculation for each keyframe. I'm continuing to work through the leg kinematics for each phase angle of the walk cycle, computing the knee position by finding the foot target, the hip-to-foot distance, and using the law of cosines to get the knee angle, then verifying each shin segment length checks out against the expected bone length. Completing shin check at 50.1 offset, giving 72.0 ✓. I continue through θ=270° and θ=315°, computing foot position, base angle, and knee offset for each, verifying the shin length stays at 72 throughout. Now I'm about to tabulate these knee and foot positions as keyframes against crank angle θ for the left leg. I need to confirm the rotation direction matches SVG's convention so the foot angle θ increases correctly with time, which it does since clockwise visual motion corresponds to positive rotation with y pointing down. For the leg animation I'll need nine keyframes spanning θ=0° through 360° (with 360° equal to 0°) so the repeating animation loops smoothly without a jump, using evenly spaced keyTimes synced to the crank's linear rotation over the full cycle duration. Now I'm thinking about how to represent the thigh and shin as a single connected polyline path. Each leg's knee and foot positions at every 45° increment need to be computed, with the right leg simply offset 180° in phase from the left, so I can derive its keyframes by reusing the left leg's values shifted by four steps. I also need to decide the draw order so the legs appear in front of the wheel where the pedals cross through the wheel's circular region, while the wheel itself stays behind. For the feet, I'm designing a small rounded shoe shape positioned at each pedal location, and since the shoe lives inside the rotating crank group, I need a counter-rotation so the shoe stays visually horizontal instead of spinning with the crank. Actually, a simpler path: I'll separate the feet from the crank group entirely and move them with animateMotion along a circular path around the hub, keeping rotate at 0 so they never tilt. I'm working out the arc path syntax to make sure the sweep direction matches clockwise pedaling motion on screen. With that confirmed, I'm setting the left foot to begin at t=0 and the right foot 180° out of phase using a negative begin offset, which correctly places it at the opposite point in the pedal cycle. I'm also adding simple crank arm lines from the hub to each foot position so the pedals look mechanically connected to the wheel's rotation. I need to work out exactly how animateMotion translates the shoe element -- since the path coordinates are absolute, the shoe needs to be drawn centered at the origin so the motion path correctly positions it at each point along the circle. No rotation is applied during the shoe's motion, which is what I want, and I'll set the spokes and crank group to rotate together around the wheel's center over the 3-second cycle. For the legs, I'm using attribute animation on the path's "d" values with matching command structure across keyframes, offsetting the right leg's phase from the left so they alternate naturally. Computing right leg coordinates... I confirm the right-leg keyframe values match shifting the left-leg sequence by index 4, consistent with the right foot starting at θ=180 at t=0. I verify the shoe's animateMotion offset timing produces the same phase shift, and double-check that the crank rotation direction aligns with the left foot reaching (400,360) at θ=0. Then I check the ground scroll speed against the wheel's circumference to confirm both move at 180px/s, keeping the rolling motion visually consistent. Now I'm sketching the anteater's upper body: positioning the hip and shoulders, then shaping the torso as a leaning ellipse rotated slightly forward to suggest a hunched, pedaling posture. Adding the signature black-and-white shoulder stripe using a clip path, then placing the head above the torso with an elongated snout angled upward, as if watching the juggled bottles. Next I'm working on the tail: a bushy, animated shape that sways gently via rotation at its base, giving the anteater a lively, swinging back end. For the arms, I'm positioning the shoulders, elbows, and hands to create raised juggling poses, with small claw details on the hands and plans to animate them moving up and down to catch items. For the arm motion, I'll rotate each arm group around its shoulder pivot with alternating oscillation so the two arms move opposite each other, mimicking a juggling rhythm. Then I'm mapping out the bottle-throwing arcs, having them travel from hand to hand in a high curve peaking near the top of the canvas. I realize a simple back-and-forth over the same apex doesn't quite capture a real cascade, since each ball should cross via a shared peak but travel distinct hand-to-hand paths rather than retracing itself—I'll need to pick slightly different control points per arc to keep the throws looking believable. Actually that back-and-forth along the same arc is realistic—in real juggling, the ball traces the same curve in both directions since it's just thrown and caught between the same two points, so having three bottles offset in phase along that single arc should look convincingly like juggling. That matches real juggling visually, with balls tracing overlapping arcs like a cascade pattern. For three bottles, I'll stagger their loop timing by a third of a second each, so each bottle cycles between left and right hands every second while being offset from the others to create the classic 3-ball cascade rhythm. Working through the timing: each ball's full cycle is 2 seconds covering two flights of 2/3s with 1/3s dwells at each hand, so each bottle's animation should alternate a 2/3s arc, a 1/3s pause, then the return arc, repeating on a 2s loop. Since this is getting too physics-precise for the visual effect, I'll simplify by giving all three bottles the same two-arc looping path with a shorter duration, around 1.2s, staggered with offsets so they're evenly spaced — accepting a less exact but still visually convincing juggling cascade. Working through the arc math, I realize the two-arc phase structure means balls at phase 1/3 and 2/3 both land near the right side rather than being evenly distributed, which doesn't match the staggered throw/catch timing of a real cascade — the offsets between balls need to correspond to even thirds of the full throw cycle, not just equal phase fractions. Mapping out ball A's full 2-second cycle: flight left-to-right, dwell at right, flight right-to-left, dwell at left. Working out how balls B and C offset in time, realizing they cross each other mid-flight in the classic cascade pattern, confirming this matches standard three-ball juggling. This all checks out — each ball has a 2s period with staggered offsets of 2/3s, so the three balls' L-throws land exactly at 0, 2/3, and 4/3, matching the R-throws at 1/3, 1, and 5/3. Now I'm working out the animateMotion timing for each ball's path — a 2s loop with two arcs (flights) and two dwell periods when the ball rests in a hand. Mapping real time fractions to path-length fractions, I need keyPoints and keyTimes values that pause the ball at the path's midpoint and endpoint during the dwell intervals, using linear interpolation between flight segments. I'm checking the apex height for the arc works out correctly. For the arm positioning, I'm debating whether to animate the juggler's arms rotating to match hand positions, or keep them mostly static with subtle bobbing for simplicity — leaning toward static arms since syncing rotation with throw/catch timing adds complexity without much visual payoff. Now I'm designing the bottle shapes: small rounded-rectangle bodies with narrow necks and caps, colored green with highlights, sized to look proportional against the arms. I'm adding an inner rotation so bottles spin while airborne, nesting it with the outer arc motion so each bottle completes a full flip during flight, then giving each bottle its own color—green, blue, orange—so they're distinguishable mid-toss. I'm also pinning the bottles to the hand positions during the dwell phase so they visually appear caught, and working out precise shoulder, elbow, and hand coordinates on the rotated torso to get the arm geometry right for the juggling pose. Now I'm computing the quadratic Bezier arc path for each bottle's throw—setting hand positions at either side of the head and solving for the control point so the apex reaches just above the figure's head. I'm staggering the three bottles with offset begin times so they're evenly phased along the same looping path, creating the classic juggling cascade rhythm. Confirming the math checks out: at t=0, A is at phase 0 (starting the L throw), B is at phase 2/3 (having just arrived back at L after its dwell), and C is at phase 1/3 (arriving at R). I verify this against the keyTimes mapping for the arcs and dwells, confirming each ball's position in its throw cycle lines up correctly with the overall juggling pattern. I'll set up the keyPoints and keyTimes so each flight segment matches equal arc lengths, with the path attribute defining the same curve. The dwell pause at the hand happens while the bottle keeps spinning, and since the arc apex sits well above the head, drawing bottles on top won't cause any visual overlap issues. Now I'm sketching the anteater's features: hands as small clawed ellipses at the catch points, then the head with a rounded skull, an elongated curved snout tapering to a dark nose tip, a small black eye with a glint, and a thin pink tongue flicking from the snout's end. I'm deciding to skip the animated tongue flick for simplicity, and planning the torso as a rotated ellipse with a thick diagonal black stripe running across the back to mimic the giant anteater's signature marking, plus a lighter belly patch I'll likely leave out. Now I'm working through the full z-order of the scene from back to front: sky, hills, ground with dashed lines, the tail tucked behind the wheel, the rotating wheel and rim, the frame/seat, the rotating crank group, and finally the legs with the back leg shaded darker for depth. I'm figuring out the layering for the rider's limbs and head — back leg before torso, front leg after it, then the shoes with motion paths, followed by the back arm behind the torso and front arm in front, with the head and juggling bottles rendered last on top. Still positioning frame parts... Adding wheel rim and spokes... Computing spoke endpoints... I'll draw the hub circle over the six spoke diameters so the rotation group spins them together like a wheel, and add a small red dot on the rim to give a visual cue of rotation. Now I'm building the ground: a base rect with a darker top edge, then two dashed lines offset in width and animated so they scroll seamlessly at the same speed as the wheel's rotation, matching the wheel's contact point at y=450. I'm extending the lines beyond the canvas edges so the dash pattern loops cleanly, and adding a soft shadow ellipse beneath the unicycle for grounding. For the sky, I'm setting a vertical gradient from blue to pale white, placing a glowing sun in the upper right, and working out cloud movement so they drift slowly leftward relative to the rider's rightward motion, positioning them offscreen at the start/end of their loop to avoid a visible jump.
